title: Saving the Humanities the Right Way Green Daily News, August 16, 2026
author: Gary Houchens
source: Gary Houchens' Substack (garyhouchens.substack.com); originally a column for the Bowling
summary: Gary Houchens, writing both for his Substack and as a newspaper columnist, uses a recent Vanderbilt/Washington University commission report to argue that the university humanities have substituted political litmus tests for scholarly ones, and that this failure is what is fueling the growth of the K-12 classical education movement. The commission, chaired by NYU philosopher Paul Boghossian, found that fields like anthropology have explicitly redefined their disciplinary mission as political activism rather than truth-seeking scholarship, a shift Houchens traces to postmodern skepticism about the possibility of objective knowledge. He is careful to note the report's own caution that this is not simply a complaint about left-leaning professors, since politically motivated intrusions from the right pose an equal threat to genuine inquiry. Houchens then pivots to argue that the explosive growth of classical Christian and classical K-12 schools reflects unmet parental demand for exactly what the university humanities once offered: an honest, truth-oriented encounter with the great texts and permanent human questions. The piece closes by framing the humanities' rescue not as an ideological realignment but as a recovery of their original purpose: disciplined, humble pursuit of truth about the human condition.
points: Cites a Vanderbilt/Princeton-scholar commission (chaired by Paul Boghossian) finding that fields like anthropology have explicitly redefined their mission as political activism rather than scholarship.
Traces the root cause to postmodern skepticism about objective truth, which the commission argues legitimizes evaluating scholarship on political rather than evidential grounds.
Notes the commission's own caution that this is not a one-sided complaint: right-wing political intrusion into curriculum is flagged as an equally corrosive risk.

Argues the K-12 classical education movement's explosive growth reflects parents seeking the honest encounter with permanent questions that university humanities once promised but increasingly fail to deliver.
quotes: History, literature, philosophy, theology, and the arts help us understand what it means to be human and how to pursue and achieve a life worth living.
The team was charged with assessing the state of scholarship in the humanities and humanistic social sciences. Their findings are sobering.
Scholars in these fields have for many years now substituted political criteria for scholarly ones in the evaluation of academic work.
Once that move is made, the humanities ceased to be a truth-seeking enterprise and became an ideological one, enforcing acceptable conclusions rather than pursuing contested ones.

The K-12 classical education movement, which emphasizes the great texts of Western civilization, genuine formation in virtue and civic life, and the unembarrassed pursuit of truth and beauty, has grown explosively in recent years.
They will be saved by recovering what they were always supposed to be: a disciplined, rigorous, humble pursuit of what is true about the human condition.
